baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Winter’s study of Great War mourning connects memory research to war’s cultural aftermath
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Remembrance becomes an object of historical inquiry; not all military history is memory studies. The checked introduction questions a clean modernist rupture and explicitly limits transfer to later catastrophes. This specifies a contribution to military/war history without identifying it with operational history.
baseline_incident_edges.map_label: Winter: mourning after the Great War

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Examines how art, museums and silence mediate remembrance of modern war.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview treats memory through changing forms of representation; remembrance is not equated with accurate or therapeutic recovery.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Contributes to the Historial museum’s international research and display of the Great War.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own museum answers explain proposing a research centre and a wider war history, with many collaborators; he is not credited as sole creator.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Teaching overlap: Prost and Winter explicitly share a contextual, cross-national and cross-theme approach to the historiography of the Great War.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Editorial undirected comparison grounded in their joint methodological argument, not coauthorship alone or a claim that either caused the other’s approach. Their introduction identifies public and professional contexts, rejects narrow thematic/national boundaries and expressly accepts mutual responsibility for two voices. Selected English second-edition introduction 2020 read; French 2004 and English 2005 originals and complete 2020 book unread. The introduction also states exclusions and the need for wider coverage; no exhaustive global scope is claimed.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Provides Winter with research and ideas on war memorials that Winter develops and qualifies, in Fitzpatrick’s reading.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: The signed review paragraph beginning The engrossing discussion says Winter develops work by Mosse, Bushaway, Inglis and Prost, then explains a particular corrective. Co-credits and Fitzpatrick mediation remain. This is a specified use of memorial research, not agreement with every political interpretation or direct testimony from Winter’s unread1995 book.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Distinguishes memorials’ initial work of consolation from later political appropriation, qualifying Mosse’s emphasis on masking the realities of war, as Fitzpatrick explains.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Fitzpatrick’s following sentence in the same long paragraph explicitly calls Winter’s primary-function emphasis a corrective to Mosse and Bushaway while preserving political uses. The review quotes Winter’s94–96, but those original pages were not independently read. Prost receives explicit precedent credit. No claim that all memorials were apolitical, every Mosse argument false, or Winter’s survey exhaustive.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Winter uses Benjamin’s angel of history to frame tradition and change in Great War remembrance
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The publisher’s reprinted conclusion opening explicitly invokes thesis IX. This supplies a named reception mechanism for the inherited Benjamin link; it is not an influence claim about every memory scholar or the Frankfurt School as a whole.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Great War memory in interwar Canada
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Vance’s Death So Noble examines Canada’s collective memory of the Great War in the 1920s and 1930s as a cultural and philosophical force (publisher description). A contribution to the memory entry’s war_mourning strand alongside Winter; no claim that Vance derives from Winter. Cook (2006) extends the question to historians’ own role. PhD context: Death So Noble is cited by 67 PhDs 2009–2026, the most of any work by this roster.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Vance: memory of the Great War

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Climate change and the collapse of the distinction between natural and human history: humans as geological agents, species history and the history of capital (2009), developed into a distinction between globe and planet (2015–22)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Dated 2009, after the atlas's 1920–2000 frame: drafted after the user's decision of 2026-10-14 to end the 2000 break. No claim here concerns his work before 2000. 'The Climate of History: Four Theses', Critical Inquiry 35, no. 2 (Winter 2009), pp. 197–222, read in full. The first thesis: 'Anthropogenic Explanations of Climate Change Spell the Collapse of the Age-old Humanist Distinction between Natural History and Human History' (p. 201). His readings in 'globalization, Marxist analysis of capital, subaltern studies, and postcolonial criticism ... had not really prepared me for making sense of this planetary conjuncture' (p. 199). On environmental history: 'the rise of environmental history in the late twentieth century made the breach wider', but 'environmental history, where it was not straightforwardly cultural, social, or economic history, looked upon human beings as biological agents', quoting Crosby's preface to The Columbian Exchange (p. 205); 'Scholars writing on the current climate-change crisis are indeed saying something significantly different from what environmental historians have said so far ... Humans now wield a geological force' (p. 206); the distinction between human and natural histories, 'much of which had been preserved even in environmental histories that saw the two entities in interaction—has begun to collapse' (p. 207). 'The mansion of modern freedoms stands on an ever-expanding base of fossil-fuel use' (p. 208). 'A critique that is only a critique of capital is not sufficient' (p. 212), yet 'the story of capital ... cannot be denied by recourse to the idea of species' (p. 219); the task is 'to mix together the immiscible chronologies of capital and species history' (p. 220). He ends with a 'negative universal history' (p. 222). Reception after 2009, labelled by date: Robert Emmett and Thomas Lekan, eds., Whose Anthropocene? Revisiting Dipesh Chakrabarty's 'Four Theses' (RCC Perspectives 2016/2, from a February 2015 workshop; read in part): the essay 'has become a primary text for understanding the problematic nature of the Anthropocene as a cultural category' (p. 7) and challenges 'ecological histories that situate humans as biological agents' (p. 8). The environmental historian Timothy J. LeCain (2016) writes, tentatively, that the theses 'may prove more radical than even he intended, or perhaps desires' (p. 15). Criticism: in his 2016 response Chakrabarty concedes to Carol Boggs that 'one can no longer separate the biological agency of humans from their geological agency in the way in which I appeared to do' (p. 104), and reports that 'Andreas Malm and Alf Hornborg took me to task' over 'There are no lifeboats for the rich', quoting Kathleen McAfee: 'Contra Chakrabarty, the rich may face the same storms and they do have lifeboats' (p. 108). Malm and Hornborg (2014) are known here through their abstract, which holds that "Intra-species inequalities are part and parcel of the current ecological crisis", and through his reports; the body of their article is unread. A contribution that disputes the field's prior framing of human agency, not a founding claim for climate history. Later work, added in revision 1.151: the Tanner Lectures (2015, read in part) distinguish humanity as "homo" from the scientists' "anthropos" and conclude that "we have fallen into 'deep' history"; The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021; publisher's page and contents; unread) is summarised in his own words: "The global is anthropocentric while the planet de-centers and provincializes the human" (Review of Politics, 2022, p. 593). In environmental history's own journal, Atte Arffman (Environment and History, 2022, read) writes that "historians can no longer dismiss material realities and non-human world" and that "not many have delved as deep as Chakrabarty does". The criticisms of the species category and of the divide's novelty are now drawn separately (environment → Chakrabarty; science → Chakrabarty).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: A call to study ‘the history of both women and men’ and ‘the significance of the sexes, of gender groups’, quoted by Joan Scott as an early relational use of gender (1975–76; Scott 1986)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: A reader’s explicit claim, read. Scott, ‘Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis’, AHR 91:5 (1986), p. 1054: those who wanted ‘a relational notion’ used ‘gender’; ‘Thus Natalie Davis suggested in 1975, “It seems to me that we should be interested in the history of both women and men, that we should not be working only on the subjected sex any more than an historian of class can focus entirely on peasants. Our goal is to understand the significance of the sexes, of gender groups in the historical past.”’ (n. 4, citing Feminist Studies 3, Winter 1975–76, p. 90). Davis’s 1976 article is unread; her words are as Scott quotes them. Her own retrospect (1997, p. 16, read) describes the same programme: ‘examining the range of relations between and concepts about women and men in different times and places’. The Holberg committee (2010, read): ‘Her work brings gender to the fore’. A precursor statement taken up in Scott’s argument, not a claim that Davis founded gender history or shared Scott’s later theoretical position.
